title: India's Direct Selling Industry Hits Rs 23,522 Crore With 91 Lakh Sellers
excerpt: The ADSEI-Kantar report counts nearly 43 lakh women among India's active direct sellers, projects Rs 25,000 crore in FY26 — and admits retention, not recruitment, is the industry's weak point.
body:
• India's direct selling industry reached Rs 23,522 crore in FY25, growing at a 7% compound annual rate, according to the ADSEI-Kantar report released in New Delhi.
  • About 91 lakh Indians are active direct sellers; 47% — nearly 43 lakh — are women, and 69% are aged 25-44.
  • The industry is projected to cross Rs 25,000 crore in FY26, and India ranks 11th among the world's 15 largest direct selling markets.
  • The constraint is spending per person: roughly $2 per capita in India against $8-12 in the lowest-spending top-10 markets — headroom, if sellers can be retained long enough to build businesses.

India's direct selling industry reached Rs 23,522 crore in the financial year ended March 2025, growing at a compound annual rate of 7%, according to the Direct Selling Industry Report by the Association of Direct Selling Entities of India (ADSEI) with research partner Kantar, released at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on Monday. The report estimates 91 lakh active direct sellers and projects the industry will cross Rs 25,000 crore in FY26, The Hindu BusinessLine reported.

Who the sellers are

Women account for 47% of active sellers — nearly 43 lakh people — and the report positions the model as a livelihood platform for women in semi-urban and rural areas, citing low capital requirements, flexible hours and no formal qualification bar. About 69% of sellers are aged 25-44, and more than 32% report consistent month-on-month income. ADSEI president Dr Sanjeev Kumar said the industry aligns with the government's focus on self-employment, skilling and women-led development, and that the association will remain a partner in "deepening compliance and consumer trust."

Where the money concentrates

The structure underneath the headline is uneven. Wellness, personal care and cosmetics account for more than 86% of sales. Six companies, each with revenue of at least Rs 1,000 crore, held about 68% of industry revenue, while companies under Rs 10 crore made up roughly 83% of the company base. North India is the largest region with a 26.8% share, followed by West India at 24.5%. ADSEI patron Gautam Bali said the earnings support household expenses, children's education, healthcare and savings for many sellers — and flagged the industry's weak point plainly: many sellers leave before their businesses find their feet, making retention, training and consumer protection the sector's priorities.

The headroom argument

India ranks 11th among the world's top 15 direct selling markets despite having the largest population of potential sellers — because spending per person is low, at around $2, against $8-12 in the lower-spending markets in the global top 10, ADSEI said. That gap is the industry's growth case: if per-capita spending merely converges part-way, the market multiplies without needing more sellers. The Consumer Protection (Direct Selling) Rules, 2021, are the regulatory frame the report credits with formalising the sector.

What it means for readers weighing it

For diaspora families, direct selling surfaces in two ways: relatives in India earning through it, and NRI networks pitched on the same model abroad. The report's own numbers supply the due diligence — only about a third of sellers report consistent monthly income, and the association itself names early dropout as the core problem. Treat any pitch accordingly: the industry is real and growing at 7% a year, but the median experience is a side income, not a salary.

What's next

ADSEI's Rs 25,000 crore FY26 projection will be testable within the year. The figures to watch are seller retention and per-capita spending — the two numbers that decide whether direct selling becomes a durable income channel for its 43 lakh women sellers or stays a high-churn supplement.
